doc.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021

chapter: Army, Miles Davis and George Benson
title: Struggling beside Benson and Sonny Stitt's mentoring
summary: He cried nightly comparing himself to Benson; Sonny Stitt took him under his wing and later asked how to reach Bill Easley.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: I’m trying to imagine your thinking about yourself when you were doing those two years with George Benson. Were you happy with your playing?

No. I’d go home and cry every night, you understand? Because George displays all the, George is just — and I was trying to play as many notes as he was and trying to be as technically proficient. And George is one of the greatest players. You know Jimmy Smith, I hung out with Phineas Newborn Jr. I’ve been around giants you understand? So I know the difference between a giant and a regular player. I got to, say for instance Sonny Stitt took me under his wings maybe about that time or whatever, and I used to hang with Sonny, and I’d try to pick Sonny’s brain. And one time I, you know we were playing two weeks in a club uptown. And we’d gotten to be close and he liked me, and kind of thought I was — so I’d asked him what he was thinking and so and so, and then he asked me a few questions — he’d say for instance but you play “I Got Rhythm” and you get to the bridge and what’s the first — and he saw me, I couldn’t go like [snaps fingers]. So he looks at me very surprised. And he says, “You mean you don’t know?” And I said, “Well not really.” And he looked and he said, “Well don’t worry about it then.” Because he knew I could play but I just didn’t know what I was doing. You know. But Sonny used to, when we’d hang out and talk and I’d be in his hotel room and we’d play and we’d go over things, Sonny Stitt would — and Sonny was very stern just like the character of Billy Mitchell or whatever. Some of those guys man were very stern. Sonny Stitt would look me right in my face and he’d say, “Bill Easley,” you know, “you’re a pretty good saxophone player but I am a master.” And I’d say, “Well yeah, Sonny, I pretty much know that.” You know. So way back then I’ve always been pretty comfortable that Sonny Stitt thought I was pretty good, man. I still don’t have any desire to be a master. But

Sonny Stitt thought I was pretty good you know. Years and years and years later I was living in Memphis, Tennessee and Sonny comes through Memphis and he would travel and play with local rhythm sections and so — but I hadn’t seen Sonny in a long time. And by this time I’ve got a foot of hair and platform shoes and a full beard. And so I go back to the dressing room after the gig to see Sonny Stitt you see. And Sonny Stitt had just come out of being in a coma for 13 days. 13 days he was in a coma. But the thing is you’ve got to get back to work because you’ve got to work. You understand? He’s got to make money so he’s back out working. And so I go back and he’s telling me about being in this coma and the fact that he couldn’t remember anything of those 13 days. And we’re talking and talking about this and talking about different things. I got ready to leave and I’m walking out of the dressing room and Sonny Stitt says to me, he says, “Hey man,” he says, “can you tell me how I can get in touch with Bill Easley?” I said, “Well I am Bill Easley.” You know. And it was like one of them “Twilight Zone” moments. And I’m thinking man, Sonny Stitt is looking for me you know. So it was what I call one of my mountaintop moments.
